title: Cloud Accounting Software: A Practical Selection and Implementation Guide
description: A buyer's guide to cloud accounting software: compare reporting, bank reconciliation, invoicing, permissions, integrations, data portability, and the controls needed for your business.
author: Emily Nakamura

sections.title: Map your accounting workflow
sections.body: Start with the work the system must support: general ledger, accounts payable and receivable, invoicing, expenses, bank reconciliation, payroll handoff, inventory, tax reporting, and month-end close. Separate mandatory requirements from conveniences. A freelancer, a multi-entity business, and an inventory-heavy retailer can have very different needs, so do not choose based on a generic feature count. Ask the accountant or finance owner to map the current workflow and identify the manual steps that cause delays or errors.

sections.title: Verify regional and tax fit
sections.body: Accounting rules, tax filings, invoice requirements, and supported currencies differ by country and business structure. Confirm that the product supports your legal entity, tax regime, fiscal-year settings, local reporting, and required invoice fields before entering real records. If an accountant or external firm must access the books, verify their preferred workflow and permission model. Treat a vendor's general statement of international availability as a starting point, not proof of local compliance.

sections.title: Evaluate reconciliation and reporting
sections.body: Test bank-feed availability for your actual bank accounts, how duplicate transactions are handled, and whether reconciliation rules can be reviewed before posting. Build a small sample of your key reports: profit and loss, balance sheet, cash flow, aged receivables, and tax summaries where applicable. Check whether reports can be filtered by entity, project, department, or tracking category if your business needs those dimensions. Ask whether closed periods can be locked and who can reopen them.

sections.title: Check controls and auditability
sections.body: Finance software should support role-based access, approval flows appropriate to the company's size, clear transaction history, and separation of duties where required. Test how a changed invoice, deleted transaction, or edited vendor record appears in the audit trail. Confirm multifactor authentication and available identity controls for the plan you would buy. For sensitive financial data, review data-processing terms, backups, retention, support access, and the process for responding to a security incident.

sections.title: Calculate the full cost
sections.body: Compare the total cost of the plan you actually need, not just the advertised entry price. Include users, entities, payroll or inventory modules, payment processing, bank-feed charges, integrations, implementation, accountant access, training, and support. Confirm whether billing is per organization, user, transaction, or feature, and whether annual billing is required to obtain the quoted rate. Ask the vendor how pricing changes when you add users or exceed usage limits.

sections.title: Plan migration and acceptance
sections.body: Before switching, export a trial copy of the chart of accounts, contacts, open invoices, bills, tax settings, and opening balances. Reconcile trial balances and a sample of historical transactions with the source system, then test permissions and approval flows. Agree on a cutover date, decide how historical records will remain accessible, and keep a rollback plan until the first close is completed. Do not go live until the finance owner signs off on reconciled balances and required reports.

sections.title: Prepare a vendor evaluation
sections.body: Ask vendors to demonstrate your own representative workflows rather than a polished generic demo. Provide a checklist for entering a bill, reconciling a bank transaction, correcting an invoice, closing a period, and exporting records. Record how many steps each task takes, what permissions are needed, and whether the audit history is understandable. Include the accountant and the person who will maintain the chart of accounts in the evaluation, since a tool that looks simple to a business owner may create extra work during month-end close.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria for go-live
sections.body: Set objective conditions before migration begins: opening balances reconcile, a sample of invoices and bills matches the source, required reports can be produced, user permissions are approved, and backups or exports have been tested. Assign one owner to sign off on each item. Keep a record of known differences and how they will be handled. Schedule the first close with enough support available, and do not decommission the old system until retention obligations are understood and the new workflow has been accepted.
